It's complicated.

As you pointed out, sometimes prices fall from productivity improvements, like we've seen in the tech sector. Ballpoint pens used to be expensive luxury items and today they are cheaper than candy. Productivity gains are great for the economy and the lower prices that result are a major benefit.

On the other hand, when prices start to fall across the board, watch out. When vendors in different sectors are lowering prices at the same time, that often means that their stuff just isn't selling very well. If that persists, expect job losses to follow, and expect those loses to exacerbate the problem.

Sometimes there's a happy explanation for it; the tax cuts, for example, might cause a brief period of general deflation, and that will look very much like an economy-wide productivity gain. Sometimes the explanation is not so happy - maybe we're in a recession, or maybe our overseas customers can't pay their bills any more. It depends on what's causing the deflation, and how long and deep the deflation goes.

Keep in mind that inflation helps debtors, and hurts lenders. It's great to borrow a million dollars worth of purchasing power today, and pay back half a million in purchasing power twenty years from now. Deflation is the opposite, it hurts people who are in debt, and helps lenders. The guys who hold the mortgages and the student loans and the credit card debt are happy to be repaid in ever-stronger dollars.

The entity that usually benefits from inflation is the entity that gains seigniorage on the currency - the government. They print money, buy stuff, and basically get the stuff for free, while their debt is paid by a sort of tax on everyone who holds now-devalued dollars. This is a large part of what's unfolding in Venezuela right now, the government is printing money to pay its bills, and its currency has become almost worthless.
